title: Design a News Feed
oneLiner: The Twitter/Facebook home timeline as a 45-minute design round: fan-out, the celebrity problem and ranking.
keyTakeaway: Feeds are read far more than they're written, so you precompute them, but pushing every post into every follower's feed is unaffordable for accounts with millions of followers. The standard answer is a hybrid: fan-out on write for ordinary accounts, fan-out on read for celebrities, merged at read time.
explanation:
Same format as the URL shortener walk-through: read the prompt, write your own answer for each stage before revealing the model answer, then tick the points you covered. The stages follow the 45-minute flow (requirements, estimation, API, data model, high-level design, deep dives, wrap-up), and the timing next to each stage is a budget, not a suggestion.

This problem is about one number. With 200 million posts a day and an average of 200 followers, copying each post into every follower's feed means about 40 billion feed writes a day, and a single post from an account with 100 million followers is 100 million writes on its own. The estimation stage is where you should discover that, and the deep dive is where you resolve it: compare fan-out on write and fan-out on read, then argue for the hybrid.

Two questions in the requirements stage change everything, so interviewers watch for them: is the feed chronological or ranked, and how skewed is the follower distribution? Ranking adds a multi-stage scoring pipeline with its own latency budget; heavy skew forces the celebrity special case. As before, you're graded on clarifying the problem, stating trade-offs out loud, using real numbers, and adapting when the interviewer pushes on a weak spot ("what happens when a user comes back after six months?").
